answer.description: Empty string when outcome is insufficient_context
answer.title: Answer

proposals.description: Returned WITH the answer rather than from a second endpoint: a separate call would re-run retrieval and split the trace across two requests. Spring's governance flow decides whether any of these execute; nothing here has run
proposals.title: Proposals

candidates_before_threshold.description: Distinct candidates AFTER duplicate collapsing, BEFORE min_score
candidates_before_threshold.title: Candidates Before Threshold

citation_source.description: `quotes` | `answer_fallback` | `none`. WHICH MECHANISM produced the citations. `quotes` is the model naming the sentence it used — the strongest evidence, and what qa-v2 is built around. `answer_fallback` is this service locating the ANSWER's own sentences in the retrieved chunks afterwards, which runs only when the model declared none: Qwen2.5-0.5B keeps to the JSON envelope on short factual questions and abandons it on open-ended ones, so a 0.73-overlap answer was shipping with zero sources. Both ship the DOCUMENT's words; they are not equally strong evidence, and a surprising citation must be traceable to the weaker mechanism
citation_source.title: Citation Source

collapsed_duplicates.description: Rows dropped as byte-identical duplicates of a higher-ranked chunk. Without this number, collapsing is invisible: a top_k of 5 that returns 2 chunks looks identical to a corpus with only 2 matches
collapsed_duplicates.title: Collapsed Duplicates

dropped_citations.description: IDs the model cited that were not in the retrieved set. Removed in code, not trusted. qa-v1 ONLY: under qa-v2 the model never states an identifier, so this list is always empty and dropped_quotes carries the signal instead
dropped_citations.title: Dropped Citations

dropped_proposals.description: Tool proposals rejected before they left this service — unknown tool, arguments that failed validation, or a document_id outside allowed_document_ids. Same rule as citations: a small model's output is checked in code, never trusted
dropped_proposals.title: Dropped Proposals

dropped_quotes.description: Quotes the model attributed to the context that could not be matched back to any chunk shown — paraphrase, invention, or an ambiguous tie between two chunks. Under qa-v2 this is the real drop signal: the model never states an identifier, so dropped_citations above cannot populate. Truncated to 60 characters, so it is never a channel for chunk text
dropped_quotes.title: Dropped Quotes

generation_backend.description: `local` or `gemini` — which backend ACTUALLY answered, not which was asked for. Recorded because the two differ in where the document text went: `gemini` sent the retrieved chunks to Google, `local` kept them on the machine
generation_backend.title: Generation Backend

grounding_overlap.description: Fraction of the answer's content words that appear in the chunks it was shown. An answer built from the context scores 0.58-1.00; one written from the model's training scores near zero. Reported always, so a borderline answer is visible even when it was allowed through
grounding_overlap.title: Grounding Overlap

history_turns_received.description: Turns Spring sent. 0 means a first turn or a caller not sending history
history_turns_received.title: History Turns Received

parse_path.description: How the model's reply was read. `json` — it returned a well-formed object. `salvaged_json` — the object was cut off mid-string by the token cap and the answer text was recovered from it. `text_fallback` — it ignored the format and wrote prose. `unparsed` — nothing usable. This is the single most useful field for 'why does the answer look like that?'
parse_path.title: Parse Path

quarantine_reasons.description: The phrases that triggered quarantine, capped at 60 characters each. The matched phrase only, never the chunk: a safety log that quotes the document is a data-leak channel wearing a security badge
quarantine_reasons.title: Quarantine Reasons

quarantined_chunks.description: Retrieved chunks removed before the model saw them, because they contained an instruction aimed at the model rather than information. The chunk is dropped, not the question — refusing the whole query would hand an attacker a denial of service for the cost of one uploaded file
quarantined_chunks.title: Quarantined Chunks

raw_model_reply.description: The model's verbatim output, only when the request set include_raw
raw_model_reply.title: Raw Model Reply

rejected_as_ungrounded.description: The retrieval cleared min_score but the ANSWER was not made of the retrieved text, so it was withheld and the outcome downgraded to insufficient_context. This is the guard against a confident answer with no source — the same rule as dropping an unresolvable citation, applied to the whole reply
rejected_as_ungrounded.title: Rejected As Ungrounded

retried_with_history.description: The question alone matched nothing above min_score, so retrieval ran a second time with the previous user turn prepended. Measured: anaphoric follow-ups ('tell me in detail', 'and?', 'tell me more') score 0 alone and 5 with it, while standalone questions never reach this path — which is why it is a FALLBACK and not applied unconditionally. Prepending always cost one of five slots to the stale topic on a topic change
retried_with_history.title: Retried With History

retrieved.description: EVERY retrieved chunk, including uncited ones
retrieved.title: Retrieved

routed_by.description: `keywords` | `classifier` | `silent` | `suppressed` | `failed`. WHICH HALF DECIDED, and it is a question that had no answer in the trace while routing lived in a keyword list in another service. The router is a trigger list AND a classifier over the retrieval encoder, and an operator reading a surprising proposal needs to know which one to go and look at. `suppressed` means the question was an unsupported request, so routing was not consulted at all
routed_by.title: Routed By

routed_tool.description: Which tool the router chose for this message, or null for none. Day 14b made this answerable: 'why was I offered this?' had no answer in the trace while routing lived in a keyword list in another service
routed_tool.title: Routed Tool

routing_confidence.description: The classifier's margin over its `none` probability; 1.0 for a keyword hit. A tool is only proposed when this clears 0.10, because a favourite that wins by 0.001 is not grounds to interrupt a human
routing_confidence.title: Routing Confidence

unsupported_request.description: The capability this service was asked for and does not have — 'send messages', 'browse the web', 'reveal its prompt'. Names WHICH limitation applies, because a generic refusal explains nothing and the Day 12 requirement is that the service explain its limitations clearly. Checked before retrieval, so an impossible request costs milliseconds instead of a minute
unsupported_request.title: Unsupported Request

document_id.description: Correlation only — Python does not look it up
document_id.title: Document Id

file.description: Document bytes. Spring sends them; Python never reads a filesystem
file.title: File

ordinal.description: Order within the document, 1-based. The first chunk is 1, never 0
ordinal.title: Ordinal

page.description: Page number for paged formats. Revision 7 recorded these two fields as added on Day 3 and they were NOT — the ingestion dataclass, the database column and the citation card all carry them, and only the published contract did not. Caught on Day 11c while implementing /ingest: without them every newly uploaded document would store NULL, and Day 9's 'Page N' line would be blank for uploads while working for the fixture-loaded corpus
page.title: Page

section.description: Heading or sheet name the chunk came from. Maps to document_chunks.section
section.title: Section

token_count.description: Measured with the embedding model's tokenizer
token_count.title: Token Count

Citation.description:
No `ordinal`, and no text.

`ordinal` was here until Day 7 and had NO CONSUMER — verified against all three rather
than assumed:

    citations table   -> {message_id, document_id, section, excerpt}, no ordinal column
    CitationDto.java  -> id, documentId, documentName, section, excerpt
    Type.ts Citation  -> the same five fields

Spring resolves everything it needs from `chunk_id`: the `document_chunks` row holds
the text it renders as `excerpt` and the `section` the card shows. An ordinal is
redundant for lookup and read by nobody. Same rule that removed `description` from
CreateTaskArguments on Day 2 — an extra field with no consumer is how the four-copies
drift started in Month 2.

Day 6 corrected this field's floor from `ge=0` to `ge=1` without asking whether the
field should exist at all. The correction was right on its own terms; the question was
simply not asked until Day 7.

No text either, for the Day 1 reason: Spring wrote the chunk rows and hydrates excerpts
from its own database rather than trusting this service to echo them back.

quote.description: The sentence FROM THE CHUNK that the model's quote resolved to — the document's words, never the model's. This is what a citation card shows: the whole chunk averages 1,538 characters and reaches 2,597, which is a dump rather than something a reader can inspect. Empty when no single sentence stood out, in which case Spring falls back to the stored chunk text
quote.title: Quote

Citation.title: Citation

ConversationTurn.description:
One earlier message in the same conversation.

Spring owns the `messages` table and sends these; Python stays stateless and
`session_id` remains correlation-only, never looked up. Keeping history in the REQUEST
rather than having Python query for it preserves rule R1 — this service holds SELECT on
the chunk tables and nothing else — and keeps the service a pure function of its input,
which is what makes a bad answer reproducible from the trace alone.
ConversationTurn.title: ConversationTurn

CreateTaskArguments.description:
Mirrors Spring's CreateTaskPayload exactly: title + priority, nothing else.

`description` was here and has been removed: no consumer exists. Spring's payload does
not accept it, the tasks table has no column for it, and the frontend's ActionProposal
union does not read it. An extra field with no consumer is how the four-copies drift
started in Month 2 — this one was two days old.

max_length 255 matches `tasks.title VARCHAR(255)`, so an over-long title is rejected
here rather than surfacing from Postgres as a 500.

priority.description: Matches TaskPriority. Month 2 hardcoded 'medium'; Month 3 infers it
priority.title: Priority

CreateTaskArguments.title: CreateTaskArguments

LookupKnowledgeArguments.description: Mirrors Spring's LookupPayload: a single query string.
LookupKnowledgeArguments.title: LookupKnowledgeArguments

RetrievalRequest.description:
Shared by /answer and /retrieve.

allowed_document_ids is REQUIRED and has NO DEFAULT, and an empty list is LEGAL.

  omitted -> 422. Spring always knows the answer, so omission is a Spring bug and
             should be loud.
  empty   -> a normal state (a user with no ready documents). Zero chunks, and
             outcome=insufficient_context.

Do not add `= []` here, and do not write `if allowed_document_ids:` at the query.
That branch is the leak: with it, an empty list silently becomes an unfiltered
search across every user's documents. The filter is applied unconditionally.
Spring computes this list as documents that are owned AND ready.

history.description: Earlier turns in this conversation, oldest first. UNLIKE allowed_document_ids this DOES default to empty, because absent and empty mean the same thing here — the first turn of a conversation has no history, and that is not a Spring bug. Truncated to the most recent settings.max_history_turns in code; the 50 cap is a sanity bound, not the working limit
history.title: History

include_raw.description: DIAGNOSTIC. Populates trace.raw_model_reply with the model's verbatim output before any parsing. Off by default and Spring never sets it: the raw reply can run to several KB of half-formed JSON and is of no use to a product request. It exists so 'the model said X but the user saw Y' is answerable at all — benchmarks/19 sets it
include_raw.title: Include Raw

model.description: Which generation backend answers. Omitted means the configured default, which is `local`. CHOOSING `gemini` SENDS THE RETRIEVED CHUNKS — the user's private documents — TO GOOGLE; `local` keeps everything on the machine. That is why this is per request and reported back in the trace, rather than configured once and forgotten. Retrieval, citations and every guardrail are identical either way; only the step that turns a prompt into text differs
model.title: Model

RetrievalRequest.title: RetrievalRequest

RetrieveResponse.description: No text. Spring wrote the chunk rows and hydrates excerpts from its own database.
RetrieveResponse.title: RetrieveResponse

candidates_before_threshold.title: Candidates Before Threshold

collapsed_duplicates.description: Rows dropped as byte-identical duplicates of a higher-ranked chunk. Without this number, collapsing is invisible: a top_k of 5 that returns 2 chunks looks identical to a corpus with only 2 matches
collapsed_duplicates.title: Collapsed Duplicates

history_turns_received.description: Turns Spring sent. 0 means a first turn or a caller not sending history
history_turns_received.title: History Turns Received

retried_with_history.description: The question alone matched nothing above min_score, so retrieval ran a second time with the previous user turn prepended. Measured: anaphoric follow-ups ('tell me in detail', 'and?', 'tell me more') score 0 alone and 5 with it, while standalone questions never reach this path — which is why it is a FALLBACK and not applied unconditionally. Prepending always cost one of five slots to the stale topic on a topic change
retried_with_history.title: Retried With History

retrieved.description: EVERY retrieved chunk, including uncited ones
retrieved.title: Retrieved

score.description: Cosine similarity in [-1, 1]. NOT pgvector distance
score.title: Score

SummarizeDocumentArguments.description:
TWO FIELDS WITH TWO DIFFERENT AUTHORS, which is the whole point of this class.

`chunk_ordinal` is what a MODEL may state. `document_id` is what CODE resolved it to.
Nothing produces both, and the distinction is load-bearing: this service must never ask
the model for a document id, because a UUID costs 36 tokens and measurably stops the
0.5B model citing at all, and it cannot know a filename it was never shown.

So the chain is: the model quotes a sentence -> `resolve_quote` turns the quote into a
1-based ordinal over the chunks ACTUALLY SENT -> this service looks that ordinal up in
its own retrieval result and fills in `document_id`. Every step after the quote is
arithmetic over data this service already holds.

`document_id` was missing until Day 14b and that was the gap: INTEGRATION_CONTRACT.md
§5 specified the ordinal-to-document translation, Spring's SummarizePayload needs
{documentId, documentName}, and NOTHING PERFORMED THE TRANSLATION. Jackson failed
closed on the mismatch — loudly, with "Unrecognized field", rather than nulling — so it
was latent rather than silent, but a proposal for this tool could not have been
executed by the backend it was addressed to.

Spring still derives `documentName` from its own `documents` row and RE-CHECKS
OWNERSHIP rather than trusting this field. A document id arriving over HTTP is a claim;
Spring owns that table and is the only side that can verify it.

chunk_ordinal.description: 1-based index into the chunks sent for this request. Resolved from a quote
chunk_ordinal.title: Chunk Ordinal

document_id.description: The document the cited chunk belongs to, RESOLVED IN CODE from chunk_ordinal — never stated by the model. Null only inside this service before resolution; a proposal that still has null here is dropped rather than sent
document_id.title: Document Id

SummarizeDocumentArguments.title: SummarizeDocumentArguments

ToolDefinition.description: One entry in the registry published by GET /tools.

arguments_schema.description: JSON Schema for this tool's arguments
arguments_schema.title: Arguments Schema

ToolDefinition.title: ToolDefinition

ToolName.description:
Values match Spring's ActionType enum EXACTLY — hyphens, not underscores.

ActionType writes these literal strings to PostgreSQL (`action_audit.type`), Jackson
dispatches on them via @JsonSubTypes, and the frontend's discriminated union in
Type.ts matches on them. The training tracker writes them with underscores; the
running system does not, and the running system wins. Emitting "create_task" here
would have required a translation layer whose only job is to undo a naming choice —
i.e. a fifth hand-maintained copy of the contract.
ToolName.title: ToolName

ToolProposal.description:
No id field, deliberately.

Verified against the running backend: Spring emits `"id": "act-<uuid>"` — a STRING with
an `act-` prefix, not a bare UUID — and that value becomes `action_audit.action_id`
(VARCHAR(255)) when a decision is recorded. Spring owns that row, so Spring mints the
id. A `proposal_id: UUID` here would have been a second, conflicting identity for the
same thing, and Spring would have had to discard it.

`label` is what the user actually reads on the approve/reject control: the frontend's
ActionProposal union in Type.ts requires it, and Spring currently hardcodes
"Create a tracking task for this request". Month 3 can do better than a constant, which
is why the model supplies it rather than the backend.

label.description: Shown on the approve/reject control. Maps to ActionProposalDto.label
label.title: Label

ToolProposal.title: ToolProposal

post.description:
The product path.

Three decisions here are made in code and never delegated to a 0.5B model:
  1. Whether there is enough context — scores are compared to min_score BEFORE the
     model is called. insufficient_context never reaches the LLM.
  2. Whether a citation is real — under qa-v2 the model quotes a SENTENCE and code
     resolves it to a chunk; an unresolvable quote is dropped into
     trace.dropped_quotes rather than guessed at.
  3. Whether a tool call runs — never here. This service PROPOSES; Spring's governance
     flow records a row for every decision including rejections, and only a human's
     approval has an effect.
  4. Which tool, if any, a message is asking for — decided by app.intent from the
     USER'S MESSAGE ONLY, never from retrieved text, so a poisoned document cannot
     forge a tool call.
post.summary: Grounded answer with citations and a diagnosable trace

get.description:
Never touches the models.

Liveness answers "is this process alive", not "is it useful yet". Checking the models
here would report a still-loading service as dead and get it killed mid-startup.

503.description: A model is still loading or failed to load

get.summary: Both models are loaded and usable

post.description:
Deliberately a plain `def`, not `async def`.

Extraction and embedding are CPU-bound. Inside an `async def` they would block the
event loop and take /health/live down with them — the FastAPI trap that has no Spring
equivalent, where a slow call only ties up its own thread. A plain `def` endpoint runs
in the threadpool.

Spring writes every chunk row in one transaction and only then sets the document
`ready`. A partially written document must never become retrievable.

**IMPLEMENTED ON DAY 16, AND THIS IS THE DAY THE PRODUCT PATH FIRST RAN.** Every
searchable document in the database before today was populated by
`benchmarks/11_load_fixture_chunks.py`, whose own docstring says it "DELIBERATELY BREAKS
RULE R1" and exists so Day 6 had data to measure retrieval against. The product's
ingestion path did not exist; an uploaded document stored its bytes, went to
`processing`, and stayed there. Day 11c built this and it was reverted; the only part
kept was `page` and `section` on the Chunk contract, which is why they are already here.

**NOTHING IS WRITTEN HERE AND THAT IS THE WHOLE BOUNDARY.** This service holds SELECT on
the chunk tables. It returns rows; Spring inserts them, in one transaction, and owns the
status transition. Rule R1 survives the one day it would have been most tempting to bend
— a `psycopg` INSERT here would be ten lines shorter and would put schema ownership in
two places.

**The document_id is correlation only.** It is never looked up, because looking it up
would mean this service deciding whether a document exists, which is Spring's to know.
It appears in the response so Spring can match a reply to a request, and in the log line
so a slow ingestion is traceable.

415.description: The file type cannot be extracted

422.description: The file contained no extractable text

post.summary: Bytes in, chunks and vectors out. Writes nothing

post.description:
Exists so a bad answer can be bisected into "retrieval was wrong" or "generation
was wrong", and so Day 13's golden questions can test retrieval without paying for
generation. The product path does not call this.
post.summary: Retrieval only, no generation. For evaluation, not for the product

get.description:
The registry, published rather than duplicated.

Spring needs to know what a proposal can look like in order to validate one, and the
Day 14 evaluation set needs it to assert that a tool is NOT proposed for an unrelated
request. Both would otherwise keep their own copy of the tool list — which is the
four-copies problem starting over on its fifth copy.

GET, and nothing here executes. Proposals are produced alongside an answer; execution is
Spring's governance flow, never this service.

THIS REGISTRY DESCRIBED TOOLS NOBODY PROPOSED, FOR FIVE DAYS. Until Day 14b the only
router in the system was a keyword trigger list in Spring that could emit `create-task`
and nothing else, so `summarize-document` and `lookup-knowledge` were published here,
validated by the contract and executable since Day 11 — and unreachable. Their selection
accuracy was undefined, not good.

Day 10 had measured the GENERATION model on the routing decision and found a constant
function: propose-v1 answered "none" to all nine cases including four explicit task
requests, and propose-v2 answered "create-task" to all nine including "what is the fleet
size". That retired the idea of a prompt deciding, and `app.intent` replaces it with a
CLASSIFIER over the retrieval encoder — which is a different thing entirely, and which
made both of the other two tools reachable.

AND IT HAD NO CONSUMER. A registry published so the tool list would stop being copied by
hand, that nothing ever read, prevents nothing. ToolRegistryConformanceTest in the Spring
suite is its first reader, and tests/test_intent.py is the second.
get.summary: The tool schemas this service may propose. Read-only
